headline: Quest's memory-load reduction is not 'universal across all models': under grouped-query attention, per-query-head page choices must share KV heads
claim: Quest selects pages using the current query vector, and every model it evaluates (LongChat-7B, Yarn-Llama-2-7B, Llama2-7B) uses standard multi-head attention, where each query head has its own KV head. In grouped-query attention (GQA), several query heads read the same KV head. Since Quest's premise is that critical tokens depend on the query, these heads may want different pages. The implementation then either loads the union of their Top-K pages for the shared KV head, which raises memory traffic by up to the group size, or forces one shared selection, which may drop pages some heads need. GQA also already shrinks the KV cache several times over, so attention is a smaller share of decode latency, and the end-to-end gain from making attention sparse may shrink as well. So the paper's '1/PageSize + K/PageNum' saving and its 1.74-2.23x end-to-end speedups are conditional on an MHA-style layout and a single-batch setting.

reasoning_chain.text: Quest estimates page criticality from the current Query vector and the per-page min/max Keys, and loads only the Top-K pages. The paper argues that criticality depends strongly on the query (Fig. 2, a single head of Llama-2-7B).

The memory-load ratio is derived as 1/PageSize + K/PageNum, and the paper claims this reduction is universal across all models. The KV-size example uses Num of Heads = 32 for Llama-7B (one KV head per query head).
The evaluated models are LongChat-v1.5-7b-32k and Yarn-Llama-2-7b-128k for accuracy and Llama2-7B for efficiency. End-to-end results are single-batch.

In GQA models, g query heads (commonly 4-8) share one KV head, and KV memory is read per KV head. GQA cuts KV cache size and attention memory traffic by about g compared with MHA, so attention becomes a smaller share of decode latency at a given context length.

If query heads in a group disagree on critical pages, as Quest's own query-dependence argument suggests they can, the shared KV head must serve the union of selections (traffic up to g*K pages) or one compromise selection (lower recall for some heads). Either way, the derived ratio no longer holds unchanged.

On GQA models, Quest may deliver smaller attention speedups at the same accuracy, or lower accuracy at the same budget, than the MHA results suggest. Because attention is a smaller part of latency, the end-to-end gain may shrink further. The paper's numbers should not be carried over to GQA models without new measurements.

mechanism_insight: Quest gets its savings from per-query selection, but memory is read per KV head. In MHA the two are the same unit. In GQA they come apart, so the very query-dependence that motivates Quest becomes a cost when several queries share one KV stream.
critical_link: The key question is how much the Top-K page sets of query heads in the same GQA group overlap. High overlap would make the union cheap and keep the savings; low overlap would erode them. The paper does not measure this because it evaluates no GQA model.
necessary_conditions: The target model uses grouped-query (or multi-query) attention.
Query heads within a group select substantially different critical pages.
End-to-end speedup is judged on decode latency, where attention's share has already shrunk under GQA.
defeaters: Measurements on GQA models show high overlap of per-head Top-K pages within a group.
A group-level criticality score (for example, max or sum over the group's queries) keeps accuracy at the same budget with little extra traffic.
At very long contexts (for example 128K+), attention again dominates decode even under GQA, which restores the end-to-end gain.
caveats: The paper does not discuss GQA. This label infers the consequence from the mechanism and the general GQA layout; it does not report a measured failure. Later systems may adapt Quest to GQA. The claim concerns what the paper's evidence supports, not whether such an adaptation is possible.
do_not_infer: Do not claim Quest cannot run on GQA models.
Do not state a specific slowdown factor for GQA; none was measured.
Do not treat the single-head Fig. 2 attention map as evidence about head disagreement within a group.

headline: Per-input-channel scaling is only 'free' where the inverse scale can be folded exactly into a linear producer used by that one layer
claim: AWQ protects salient channels by multiplying weight input channels by s and dividing the input by s. It relies on the division being absorbed into the previous operator, which the paper says is 'usually' possible. That fold is exact and costs nothing only if the producer of X is linear (or positively homogeneous) per channel. It also must feed only the layer whose scale is being chosen. If the producer is a non-homogeneous activation such as GELU, AWQ either cannot scale that layer exactly or must add an explicit runtime scaling step. If several layers share one input (q/k/v after one norm, parallel attention+MLP blocks, or GQA value heads feeding o_proj), they must share one scale vector. In those cases the per-layer search of Eq. 4 becomes a constrained compromise, and the protection, the zero-overhead claim, or both may be weaker than in the LLaMA/OPT setting the accuracy tables cover.

reasoning_chain.text: AWQ searches a per-input-channel scale s = s_X^alpha that minimizes ||Q(W diag(s)) (diag(s)^-1 X) - W X|| for a certain layer. The paper states that s^-1 X can usually be fused into the previous operator.

General fact: dividing X by s at no cost requires the producer f of X to satisfy f(z)/s = f'(z) for some re-parameterized f'. This holds for a norm's affine gain, for the output channels of a preceding linear layer, and for ReLU when s > 0. It does not hold for GELU-like activations: GELU(z)/s != GELU(z/s).

General fact: when one tensor feeds several linear layers (q, k, v after one normalization; attention and MLP after a shared norm in parallel-block models), there is only one place to fold the inverse scale. All consumers must therefore use the same s. Under GQA, scaling a value channel scales that channel for every query head in the group, which ties o_proj input scales across heads.

For layers fed by a non-homogeneous activation (e.g., fc2 after GELU in GPT-NeoX/Falcon/MPT/StarCoder-style MLPs), AWQ has two options. It can skip scaling, which leaves RTN-level error in that layer. Or it can insert an explicit elementwise scale, which adds a memory pass in the memory-bound decode stage that TinyChat targets. For shared-input layers, the scale that minimizes the joint error is not the per-layer optimum Eq. 4 describes.
The accuracy evaluations use OPT, LLaMA/Llama-2, Mistral/Mixtral, Vicuna, CodeLlama and the language parts of OpenFlamingo/LLaVA/VILA. Falcon, MPT and StarCoder appear only in TinyChat speed results.

If a target architecture has many layers whose inputs cannot be folded exactly, or has heavily shared inputs, two outcomes may follow. AWQ's accuracy advantage over RTN may shrink on those layers. Or keeping it may cost extra runtime ops. The reported accuracy results therefore may not transfer unchanged to those architectures.

mechanism_insight: AWQ's hardware-friendliness comes from an equivalence transform, not from the quantizer. That transform is exact and free only when the graph has a suitable linear 'slot' to absorb the inverse scale, used by exactly one consumer. The method's applicability therefore depends on graph topology and the choice of activation function.
critical_link: Whether non-foldable or shared-input layers carry enough quantization error to matter. If the affected layers are few or their error is small, skipping them or using a shared compromise scale may cost little.
necessary_conditions: The target model has linear layers whose input comes from a non-positively-homogeneous op (e.g., GELU) or from a tensor shared by several separately quantized layers.
Those layers contribute non-negligible quantization error at the chosen bit width (e.g., INT3/INT4 g128).
The comparison holds bit width, group size and calibration fixed, and contrasts architectures where the fold is exact with ones where it is not.
defeaters: Implementations scale the shared input jointly and lose little accuracy compared with per-layer scaling.
An explicit scaling op is fused into an existing kernel (e.g., the dequantization GEMM) at negligible cost.
Measurements on GELU-MLP or parallel-block models show AWQ gains comparable to those on LLaMA/OPT.
caveats: The paper says 'usually', so it does not claim universality. Weight clipping and grouped quantization still apply to non-scaled layers. Practical AWQ implementations may already handle shared inputs jointly; this label concerns what the paper's method and evidence establish, not any specific codebase.
do_not_infer: Do not infer that AWQ fails on Falcon/MPT/StarCoder; the paper simply reports no accuracy numbers for them.
Do not treat the ReLU case (OPT) as non-foldable; ReLU is positively homogeneous for s > 0.
Do not equate the shared-scale constraint with a measured accuracy loss.

headline: Why high mean-activation channels are salient is only hypothesized, so a static mean-magnitude scale may misallocate protection under activation shift
claim: AWQ ranks channel saliency by the average activation magnitude on a small Pile calibration set. It folds the resulting scale permanently into the weights. The reason these channels matter is stated only as a hypothesis: larger-magnitude features are 'generally more important'. A first-moment statistic can rank channels differently from their actual contribution to output error. This happens, for example, when a channel matters through rare, very large, token-specific activations. It also happens when deployment inputs (code, image tokens, long contexts, chat templates) activate different channels than pretraining text does. If saliency on the target distribution diverges from calibration mean magnitude, the fixed scale may protect the wrong channels. The within-Pile cross-domain test (0.5-0.6 PPL degradation on one model) does not establish how stable the pattern is under larger shifts.

reasoning_chain.text: Keeping the 0.1-1% of channels with the largest activation magnitude in FP16 recovers most of the INT3 loss, while weight-norm or random selection does not. The authors hypothesize that input features with larger magnitudes are generally more important.

The scale is s_X^alpha, where s_X is the per-channel average activation magnitude from a small Pile calibration set. alpha is grid-searched to minimize the layer output error on the cached calibration activations X. The scale is then folded into the weights offline.

General fact: a channel's contribution to output quantization error scales roughly with E[x_c^2] (times weight error), not E[|x_c|]. Heavy-tailed, token-specific activations, which are widely reported in LLMs, can make these two rankings disagree.

Toy example. Channel A has |x| = 0.1 on 99% of tokens and 50 on 1%, so its mean is about 0.6 and E[x^2] is about 25. Channel B has |x| = 1 always, so its mean is 1 and E[x^2] is 1. A mean-magnitude ranking prefers B; a squared-error view prefers A by about 25x. This is an illustrative construction, not a measurement of any model.

The robustness evidence is OPT-6.7B INT3-g128 calibrated on PubMed or Enron (both Pile subsets) and evaluated on the other. AWQ degrades by 0.5-0.6 PPL compared with matched calibration. For the VLMs, only the language part is quantized.

If deployment activations shift salient channels away from those with high calibration mean magnitude, the static scale may under-protect the newly salient channels and over-scale others. Scaling others raises error on non-salient channels, as Table 2 shows for large s. The 'minimal reliance on the calibration set' would then not imply robustness, because the stability of the activation-saliency link itself has not been established.

mechanism_insight: AWQ relies on an empirical correlation between mean input magnitude and weight importance. It never identifies the mechanism behind that correlation, such as persistent outlier channels created during pretraining. How the correlation behaves under fine-tuning, new modalities or token-specific outliers is therefore an open question rather than a property of the method.
critical_link: Whether the set of high-mean-magnitude channels is stable across the input distributions a deployed model sees. If outlier channels are persistent model properties, as is often observed, the risk is small. If they are input-dependent, the fixed scale can be misallocated.
necessary_conditions: The deployment input distribution activates salient channels that differ materially from those of Pile calibration text.
Error on those channels is not already handled by group-wise quantization (g128) and the alpha search.
Comparisons use the same bit width and model, and vary only the calibration/deployment mismatch.
defeaters: Outlier channels prove to be persistent model properties largely independent of input domain.
Reported VLM and instruction-tuned results (Tables 6-7, Fig. 5) already reflect substantial distribution shift with little loss.
Calibrating on target-domain data gives no meaningful improvement over Pile calibration.

This label does not claim AWQ is fragile, only that the reason its saliency signal works, and so its stability, is not established.

headline: Fragmentation parity with PagedAttention does not hold as tensor parallelism grows, because the minimum allocation in tokens scales with TP degree
claim: vAttention maps physical memory per worker, per layer, per K/V tensor, in page-groups of at least 64KB. With the modified driver the minimum is 64KB; with stock CUDA it is 2MB. The number of tokens in one page-group is the page-group size divided by the per-worker bytes per token (H_worker x D x P). It therefore grows in proportion to the tensor-parallel degree, and also as KV heads per worker shrink or KV precision drops. The paper's claim that vAttention is 'as effective in reducing fragmentation as PagedAttention' rests on TP-1/TP-2 configurations where 64KB holds 32-128 tokens. At higher TP degrees, with GQA/MQA models or with FP8 KV caches, the same 64KB floor may mean hundreds of tokens per allocation unit. The 2MB fallback would mean thousands. Per-request internal fragmentation, and so the maximum batch size, may then fall behind PagedAttention, whose block size in tokens is set independently of TP. Fixing this through tensor slicing gives up per-layer contiguity and requires strided-access kernels.

headline: Latency hiding for prefill allocation is weakest exactly where small pages are recommended: high memory pressure with variable prompt lengths
claim: vAttention hides the latency of CUDA VMM calls in two ways. For decode, it uses the per-iteration predictability of growth. For prefill, it reuses page-groups left behind by finished requests (deferred reclamation) and eagerly maps a few page-groups ahead. Prefill reuse covers a new request only if its prompt is no longer than the recycled slot's mapped length. Eager pre-mapping requires a pool of spare physical memory. In throughput-oriented serving near memory capacity, which is the regime where the paper recommends 64KB page-groups, both conditions may often fail. Prompt lengths vary, and the mapped-page pool is drained or reclaimed. Prefill mapping then moves back onto the critical path. That penalty is largest for 64KB pages: they have the lowest allocation bandwidth (7.6 GB/s vs 35 GB/s for 2MB) and the highest measured synchronous overhead (up to 1.15x vs 1.03x). So the fragmentation optimization and the latency optimization may partly work against each other.

reasoning_chain.text: Deferred reclamation assigns a finished request's reqId, with its mapped pages, to a new request. New allocations are needed only if the new request's context is longer. Eager allocation keeps a small number of page-groups mapped for the next reqId. Reclamation is triggered when cached page-groups fall below a threshold (e.g., 10% of GPU memory).

Synchronous allocation adds prefill overhead of up to 1.15x with 64KB pages and up to 1.03x with 2MB pages (single 16K-token prompt). Allocation bandwidth is 7.59 GB/s per GPU at 64KB vs 35.17 GB/s at 2MB (TP-1).

The paper recommends small page-groups for throughput-oriented scenarios where maximizing batch size matters. The decode-overlap ablation uses 2MB pages, batch 32 and 2K-3K prompts. The deferred-reclamation ablation uses a single 16K prompt. If step() cannot satisfy demand, the framework preempts requests.

Rough model. If prefill allocation is fully synchronous, its added time fraction is about (prefill tokens/s x KV bytes per token per GPU) / allocation bandwidth. Take Yi-6B at 64KB per token, a prefill rate on the order of 10^4 tokens/s, and 7.59 GB/s. That gives about 0.65 GB/s / 7.59 GB/s, or roughly 8-9%, which is of the same order as Fig. 13's reported overheads. This is a back-of-envelope estimate, not a measurement.

General fact: near memory capacity, a serving system keeps almost all physical memory mapped to active requests, leaving little slack for pre-mapped spare pages. Real traces (e.g., chat, summarization) have widely varying prompt lengths, so a recycled slot is often shorter than the incoming prompt.

If the server runs near capacity with 64KB pages and heterogeneous prompts, prefill may increasingly pay synchronous mapping costs, and occasionally unmapping costs when reclamation fires. TTFT and prefill throughput would then lose part of vAttention's prefill-kernel advantage over PagedAttention. Using 2MB pages to cut that cost brings back the fragmentation that 64KB pages were meant to remove.

mechanism_insight: Hiding allocation latency depends on slack, either predictable growth or spare mapped pages. Minimizing fragmentation removes slack. Because both are tuned through page-group size and the reclamation policy, the configuration that maximizes batch size is also the one where allocation is most likely to land on the critical path.
critical_link: How often, in a realistic near-capacity trace with 64KB pages, a new prefill finds neither a long-enough recycled slot nor a pre-mapped spare. The paper's ablations use single prompts or fixed-length batches and do not measure this.
